sections.history: Kaduthuruthy, in Kottayam district, was the headquarters of the Vadakkumkoor dynasty, and the Thaliyil Mahadeva Temple stands at the centre of its devotional memory. It is a thali temple, one of the old Shiva shrines of central Travancore, and is counted with Vaikom and Ettumanoor as the third of a sacred trio. Tradition remembers a Vadakkumkoor ruler who worshipped all three deities on a single day, and who is said to have arranged the Kaduthuruthy temple so that the lords of Ettumanoor and Vaikom are honoured at its southern and northern gates. The temple has served as a place of worship and community for many centuries, though its early history is not firmly dated. Less visited than its famous neighbours, it keeps a quiet, local character.
sections.architecture: The temple follows the traditional Kerala idiom: a walled precinct entered through gateway structures, a sanctum with a layered roof set within a circumambulatory court, and lamp-lined walls beneath sloping tiled roofs. The sanctum houses the lingam of Mahadeva, and the arrangement of the entrances is bound up with the tradition that the lords of Ettumanoor and Vaikom are honoured at the southern and northern gates. The compound is modest in scale compared with the great Kerala shrines, and its character comes from timber, tile and stone worn smooth by long use rather than from monumental display.
sections.legends: The legend of Kaduthuruthy belongs to the story of Khara, a demon who won three Shiva lingas through severe penance. He is said to have carried them in his hands and at his mouth or neck, and where he set them down, they remained: at Vaikom, at Ettumanoor and at Kaduthuruthy. Tradition places the lingam carried closest to his mouth or neck here, though accounts differ on the details. The three shrines are therefore revered as one connected pilgrimage, and a devotee who worships at all three on Vaikathashtami, completing the round before noon, is said to gain the merit of a pilgrimage to Kashi.
sections.festivals: The annual festival of the temple is held over ten days in the Malayalam month of Medam, around April and May. It opens with the hoisting of the festival flag, the Kodiyettu, and is marked by temple music, cultural programmes and a procession of caparisoned elephants. The temple is also visited by pilgrims who follow the Vaikathashtami round of Vaikom, Ettumanoor and Kaduthuruthy in the month of Vrischikam; confirm dates locally.
sections.experience: Kaduthuruthy offers a quieter, more local experience than the great temples of the circuit. A visit here is often part of the three-temple pilgrimage with Vaikom and Ettumanoor, which lie nearby, and the town sits in the green, watery country of Kottayam district. Expect a modest, unhurried precinct, where daily worship continues in the traditional Kerala manner and the sense of continuity matters more than scale.

visit.timings: The temple generally opens in the early morning and again in the evening, with a midday closure, as is the custom in Kerala Shiva temples. Hours change during festivals, so please confirm timings locally before travelling.
visit.dressCode: Traditional attire is expected. Men are often asked to remove upper garments and wear a mundu, and women to dress modestly in a saree or similar. Please confirm the current requirements at the temple.
visit.photography: Photography is typically restricted within the temple precincts, especially near the sanctum. Please ask staff and follow their instructions.
visit.gettingThere: The temple is in Kaduthuruthy, Kottayam district, roughly midway between Vaikom and Ettumanoor. The nearest railheads are at Kaduthuruthy, Ettumanoor and Kottayam, and the nearest airport is Kochi. The town is reached by road from Kottayam and Vaikom.
